claims.claim: Rosebury holds that Tolkien opens passages in plain modern language and modulates into a higher register only where the narrative touches ancient or magical history.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: modulating into a higher register to deal with echoes

claims.claim: Turner argues Tolkien assigns discrete linguistic registers to different peoples: simple and modern for Hobbits, more archaic for Dwarves, Elves and the Rohirrim.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Turner 2020/2022)
claims.quote: discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples

claims.claim: Shippey holds that the Hobbits' modern idiom lets them mediate between the modern reader and the heroic, archaic world of the epic.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Shippey 2005)

claims.claim: Shippey reads 'The Council of Elrond', roughly fifteen thousand words consisting entirely of talk, as a tour de force in which each of many speakers is given a distinct idiom.
claims.source: 'An Analysis of Scholarship on Tolkien: The Council of Elrond' (student synthesis of Shippey)

claims.claim: Saruman's duplicity is conveyed through politically minded, abstract modern speech.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'To Make a Soul'
claims.quote: politically minded, abstract manners of speech

claims.claim: Tolkien imagined the Rohirrim speaking the Common Speech more slowly and deliberately because it was their second language.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'To Make a Soul' (citing Tolkien's letter to Tiller)
claims.quote: much slower and more deliberate

claims.claim: Rosebury identifies three types of Orc dialogue keyed to rank; Grishnákh speaks like a melodrama villain while Gorbag uses grumbling twentieth-century bureaucratic speech.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: three types of Orc-dialogue for different ranks

claims.claim: Rosebury describes Gollum's extraordinary idiolect of obsessive repetition and infantile whining; the translation literature adds ungrammatical syntax, 'pocketses' plurals and I/we confusion.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: obsessive repetition, infantile whining

claims.claim: The Rohirrim's speech carries actual Old English words and phrases such as éored, dwimmerlaik and mearas, and the Dwarves' speech is archaic, blunt and proverbial.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'

claims.claim: Turner's example of fronting, placing the object before the verb, is 'Weapons they have laid at your doors', a construction he notes cannot be reproduced in French and is unmarked in German.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Translating The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner)
claims.quote: Weapons they have laid at your doors

claims.feature: Old English to Modern English mapping
claims.claim: Shippey explains that Tolkien rendered Rohirric as Old English so that its relation to Westron mirrors Old English's relation to Modern English.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Translating The Lord of the Rings' (citing Shippey)

claims.claim: Key semantic domains for entire/maximum, loud, hot, and long/tall/wide support the hypothesis that Tolkien tends toward hyperbole, while dense plant vocabulary (elm-tree, alder, rowan, hemlock) supplies circumstantial realism.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: Tolkien tends to resort to hyperbole

claims.claim: Lee shows from typescripts that Tolkien deliberately condensed the climactic prose into short sentences piled one on another, matching Kullmann and Siepmann's 'short, stark sentences' of the epic mode.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: Tolkien deliberately condensed the prose

claims.claim: Lee, following Kullmann and Siepmann, describes LOTR's narrator as omnipresent and heterodiegetic, less intrusive than The Hobbit's, ranging over the battlefield with the Old English poet's freedom from space and time.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: does not take part in the story

claims.claim: Rosebury shows Tolkien favouring plain descriptive phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off' over the more literary 'wear' and 'dismount', and rejects unsupported charges of archaising and wrenched syntax.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien: A Cultural Phenomenon'
claims.quote: a certain sensuous precision, distinctive of Tolkien

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann hold every poem follows a traditional genre and is fitted in style and content to its speaker, and Straubhaar that prose and verse are built to flow as an integrated whole.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Poetry in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: fitted in style and contents to the characters

claims.claim: Kullmann argues the shift from prose to poetry directs attention from meaning to sound, with hobbit verse in simple iambic tetrameter, Elvish verse in liquid l-sounds, and Rohan's in Old English alliterative metre.
claims.source: Kullmann, 'Poetic Insertions in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings', Connotations 23.2
claims.quote: direct the focus away from meaning to sound

claims.claim: Rateliff records that Tolkien's 1960 rewrite tried to bring The Hobbit into harmony with LOTR's mood, language and geography, and was abandoned because it was losing the humour and no longer read as The Hobbit.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The History of The Hobbit' (citing Rateliff, Fisher)
claims.quote: losing much of the humour

claims.claim: Kirk (1971), as summarised, treats LOTR as a philological experiment with a deliberate fairy-tale hobbit style, register graded by social standing (Frodo speaks more nobly), and a resistance to Latin-derived vocabulary.
claims.source: rogersdylan blog, 'I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish' (summary of Kirk 1971)
claims.quote: a grand philological experiment

claims.claim: The Red Book conceit, the Prologue's 'Note on the Shire Records' and the appendices produce an editorial distance mimicking historical recovery; West says the device appeals to the modern mystique of scholarly research.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Red Book of Westmarch'
claims.quote: the modern mystique of scholarly research

claims.claim: Agøy's survey of all descriptions in LOTR finds Tolkien's descriptions rarely very detailed, with characters, buildings and scenery described quite vaguely so readers complete the picture.
claims.source: Agøy 2013, 'Vague or Vivid? Descriptions in The Lord of the Rings', Tolkien Studies 10 (abstract via OpenAlex)
claims.quote: Tolkien's descriptions are rarely very detailed

claims.claim: Lee reports Rateliff's observation that Tolkien often describes a scene not as experienced but as remembered afterwards, and that Walker and Rateliff both call this the 'invitational style'.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF), citing Rateliff 2009 and Walker 2009
claims.quote: as you would remember it afterwards

claims.claim: Walker credits the prose with a sense of time that brings past and future into the present; Shippey defends the Lament of the Rohirrim as a paraphrase of The Wanderer's ubi sunt against Manlove's charge of overworked cadences.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary reception of The Lord of the Rings' (and 'Tolkien's prose style')
claims.quote: overworked cadences

claims.claim: Chen argues Tolkien's Secondary Belief is produced by a style of hypotyposis (vivid evocation), metalepsis and harmonism across LOTR and The Silmarillion.
claims.source: Chen 2014, 'Tolkien's Style of Fantasy', Caietele Echinox 26 (CEEOL abstract)
claims.quote: hypotyposis, metalepsis and harmonism

claims.claim: Lewis's 1955 review praises the romance's very high architectural quality, its two-pattern six-book design, and the fact that no individual or species exists only for the plot.
claims.source: kate_nepveu, 'LotR re-read: Lewis, The Dethronement of Power'
claims.quote: very high architectural quality

claims.claim: Lobdell argues the architecture and narrative style of the Edwardian adventure story (King Solomon's Mines, The Lost World) underlie The Hobbit and LOTR.
claims.source: Lobdell, The World of the Rings (Internet Archive record)
claims.quote: the Edwardian adventure story

claims.claim: Simon argues that putting Théoden's speech about dying honourably into modern idiom would require an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Simon's lesson for fantasy writers is that stylistic choices must serve the story and never call attention to themselves, or they bounce the reader out.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: bouncing one out of the story

claims.claim: Siepmann's corpus study attributes the impression of archaicity to three lexical causes: overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation (CL2017, Birmingham)
claims.quote: the avoidance of words associated with the modern world

claims.claim: Siepmann finds the key words shared with nineteenth-century novels cluster in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs, and were already obsolescent when Tolkien wrote.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing

claims.claim: Words key only to The Lord of the Rings fall into warfare, natural features (dike, fen, dingle, starless), artefacts (fastness, sheath), peoples (lore-masters, wolf-riders), time (yesteryear) and prepositions (among, outwards), jointly producing an otherworldly atmosphere.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness

claims.claim: Siepmann finds Tolkien prefers the homeliest collocations yet pairs everyday adjectives like 'great' unusually with abstractions, objects and weather, and leans on hyperbole domains (entire/maximum, loud, heavy, tall).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: a marked preference for the most homely collocations available

claims.claim: Oakley Gordon argues the archaic quality of Tolkien's dialogue lies in word order rather than vocabulary, contrasting 'Nay, Gandalf!' with 'Not at all my dear G.' and calling the older orders terser and more vivid.
claims.source: Oakley Gordon, Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing (Salka Wind, 2021-12-24)
claims.quote: terser, more vivid

claims.claim: Shippey notes Saruman, as quoted by Gandalf, talks like a politician in empty modern words (real, ultimate, deploring), the one modern register in the chapter.
claims.source: Wikipedia, The Council of Elrond (citing Shippey 2005)
claims.quote: talks like a politician

claims.claim: The course blog tabulates the Council: Glóin in short broken sentences and apposition, hobbits in quick exclamations, Aragorn slipping between Elendil's heir and Strider, Boromir in a relatively Elrondian pattern.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose (2014-04-18)

claims.claim: Rosebury (per Wikipedia) identifies at least three orc dialects by rank, with Grishnákh talking like a melodrama villain or public-school bully and Gorbag in the idiom of a murderous bureaucracy.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: like a melodrama villain, or a public-school bully

claims.claim: Turner (per Wikipedia) cites Pippin's 'O Wise People!' to Gildor as a hobbit attempting the formal register and thereby mediating it for the reader.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Turner 2020)
claims.quote: O Wise People!

claims.claim: Wilton lists revived Old English words (mathom, smial, barrow) and says Rohan's language was made to resemble ancient English so that its usages seem vaguely familiar and evoke ages past.
claims.source: David Wilton, Old English in LoTR (Wordorigins, 2020-03-07)
claims.quote: seem vaguely familiar and evoke images of ages past

claims.feature: ubi sunt echo of The Wanderer
claims.claim: Novelist Patricia Bracewell juxtaposes The Wanderer's ubi sunt formula with the Rohirrim lament to show Tolkien's prose carrying the current of Old English history and language.
claims.source: Patricia Bracewell, Tolkien and the Anglo-Saxons (2018-08-17)
claims.quote: the thrumming current of Old English history and language

claims.claim: The Universe in Words post shows the lament built on repeating a single phrase, 'Where is', each repetition conjuring one Rohirric image and conferring nostalgic value through rhetorical question.
claims.source: A Universe in Words, Tolkien, 'The Wanderer' and the Ubi Sunt-tradition (2015-11-07)
claims.quote: relies on the repetition of a single phrase

claims.claim: Drout (per Wikipedia) holds that the craftsmanship is consistent from the single sentence to the journey's macro-structure, all built on a repeated stress and release pattern.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Drout 2004)
claims.quote: a repeated stress and release pattern

claims.claim: Le Guin infers from the cadences that Tolkien must have heard what he wrote, placing him with Dickens and Woolf as writers whose narrative prose wants the living voice.
claims.source: Jason Fisher, Lingwë (2010-09-23)
claims.quote: Tolkien must have heard what he wrote

claims.claim: Le Guin, in Conversations on Writing, says short rhythms repeated form long rhythms and this cyclical repetition is why the book enchants.
claims.source: Goodreads note, Ursula K. Le Guin: Conversations on Writing
claims.quote: Short rhythms repeated form long rhythms

claims.feature: iambic vs alliterative meter in prose
claims.claim: Venkatesh's writing lesson shows iambic pentameter driving plain action prose like a drumbeat, while elevated battle passages switch to four-stress Anglo-Saxon alliterative meter.
claims.source: Krishnan Venkatesh, Rhythm: A Writing Lesson from Tolkien (The Old Pearl Bed, 2017-01-13)
claims.quote: like a drumbeat, marking the relentless forward drive

claims.claim: Venkatesh says the alliterative sections turn incantatory and trance-like, with repetition ('All is lost. All is lost') intensifying emotion, and that double-meter lets Tolkien switch modes effortlessly.
claims.source: Krishnan Venkatesh, The Old Pearl Bed (2017-01-13)
claims.quote: incantatory, almost trance-like

claims.feature: verse embedded in prose at peaks
claims.claim: Shelton (per Wikipedia) notes Éomer declaims alliterative verse mid-battle, midway between lament and battle-cry, and the chapter closes on an elegiac lay imitating Beowulf.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Battle of the Pelennor Fields (citing Shelton; Mahon 1978)
claims.quote: Mourn not overmuch! Mighty was the fallen, meet was his ending

claims.claim: Drout praises 'Speeding along with little hope of stopping or turning' as an apo koinou construction that forces tiny re-readings of the sentence's meaning.
claims.source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk (2007-04-12)
claims.quote: Speeding along with little hope of stopping or turning

claims.feature: depth via inconsistent documents in varied styles
claims.claim: Drout, Hitotsubashi and Scavera (per Wikipedia) trace the impression of depth to casual incomplete allusions and multiple inconsistent accounts written as if by different hands.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings (citing Drout et al. 2014)
claims.quote: as if by different hands

claims.claim: Sipahi (per Wikipedia) shows the Prologue frames the text as oral tradition written down, copied and redacted, so the narrator's voice is that of a translator-editor of old documents.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings (citing Sipahi 2016)

claims.claim: Auden's 1956 review concedes light comedy is not Tolkien's forte and the opening chapters are a little shy-making, while the sense of the credible is never violated.
claims.source: W. H. Auden reviews (1954, 1956; Epistle of Dude reprint)
claims.quote: light comedy is not Mr. Tolkien's forte

claims.claim: Lewis characterises the book's register as gorgeous, eloquent and unashamed heroic romance, opening lighter in a way that risks losing readers.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis reviews (1954, 1955; Epistle of Dude reprint)
claims.quote: gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed

claims.claim: Wikipedia's sound article reports Black Speech built to sound harsh with about 63% consonants and more voiced plosives against 52–55% for Elvish, which was chosen for beauty.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Sound and language in Middle-earth
claims.quote: to sound harsh

claims.feature: game design: slowness as Tolkien feel
claims.claim: Game designer Sage LaTorra argues The One Ring captures the feel of Tolkien's writing through deliberate length and slowness, its long-winded journeys and discourses, rather than mechanical elegance.
claims.source: Sage LaTorra, I Spent The Last Year Being A Hobbit (2021-07-12)
claims.quote: long-winded journeys

claims.claim: The Adventures in Middle-earth Loremaster's Guide (per its reviewer) tells game masters to keep the melancholic undertone of the long defeat, treating The Hobbit as a subjective memoir.
claims.source: rasmusnord01, Adventures in Middle-earth Loremaster's Guide review (Mindlands, 2017-10-23)
claims.quote: a melancholic undertone to Tolkien's world

claims.claim: The Wikipedia article credits Drout (2004), not Le Guin, with the 'stress and release' formulation, while crediting Le Guin (2001) only with a sympathetic account of the style.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style

claims.claim: Tolkien rejects the 'tushery' charge, holding that genuine archaic English is terser than modern English and can say things the modern idiom cannot.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 171 to Hugh Brogan (1955), quoted in 'Passages I Highlighted in The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien'
claims.quote: a real archaic English is far more terse than modern

claims.claim: Tolkien describes Théoden's dialogue as 'moderated or watered archaism', deliberately short of authentic Middle English while still non-modern.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 171, as quoted via Le Guin in TheOneRing.net, 'From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie'
claims.quote: moderated or watered archaism

claims.claim: Tolkien defines hobbits as rustic English people made small, which grounds their plain modern speech register.
claims.source: BBC Radio 4 interview with Denys Gueroult, January 1971 broadcast, transcript at uv.es
claims.quote: Hobbits are just rustic English people

claims.claim: Tolkien names Welsh style-and-sound and Finnish as the potent influences behind his nomenclature, especially mountain names.
claims.source: BBC interview with Denys Gueroult, transcript at uv.es
claims.quote: attracted me by it's style and sound

claims.claim: Tolkien says a complicated story must be worked to a map or it cannot be kept consistent.
claims.source: BBC interview with Denys Gueroult, transcript at uv.es
claims.quote: you must work to a map

claims.claim: Tolkien describes encountering a new language as like tasting a new wine, an aesthetic and nourishing pleasure underlying his invented tongues.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, ''Tolkien in Oxford' (BBC, 1968): A Reconstruction', Tolkien Studies 15 (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: just like tasting a new wine

claims.claim: Tolkien says a good deal must remain unexplained even where explanation exists, because a mythical age needs enigmas.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 144 to Naomi Mitchison (1954)
claims.quote: even in a mythical Age there must be some enigmas

claims.feature: familiar vs deferential pronouns as register marker
claims.claim: Appendix F says Shire hobbits lost the familiar/deferential distinction, so Pippin addressed even Denethor familiarly, astonishing Gondor.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Eowyn's Thee and Thou' (Sacnoth's Scriptorium), quoting Appendix F footnote
claims.quote: including the Lord Denethor himself

claims.feature: degraded orc speech / elvish command of styles
claims.claim: Appendix F notes Elves commanded many styles while Orc and Troll speech was actually filthier than shown.
claims.source: Tolkien, Appendix F, discussed at TheOneRing.net Reading Room
claims.quote: more filthy than I have shown it

claims.feature: worn-down obsolete name-stock for the Shire
claims.claim: Tolkien explains Shire names carry elements that are obsolete, dialectal or worn-down in current English, giving them antiquarian texture.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: obsolete or dialectal, or are worn-down and obscured in form

claims.claim: Tolkien identifies 'Oliphaunt' as an archaic form used as a rusticism, lamenting the loss of archaic colouring in translation.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: an archaic form of 'elephant' used as a 'rusticism'

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers debased rustic associations of 'elf' over pretty literary fancies, signalling his distaste for ornamental register.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: less damaging than the 'pretty' literary fancies

claims.claim: Tolkien's rule for heroic diction is to avoid both the colloquial and the obscure, being antiquated without being arcane.
claims.source: Philip Irving Mitchell, 'Tolkien on Translating Beowulf' (DBU)
claims.quote: intentionally antiquated but not intentionally arcane

claims.claim: Flieger describes the work's richness and multivalent texture that lets every reader take what they need.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Flieger); Flieger interview at Tolkienista
claims.quote: so rich, so multi-valent

claims.claim: Lewis praises the names as a feast that at moments embody a piercing, high, elvish beauty unmatched in prose.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis, 'The Gods Return to Earth' (Time and Tide, 1954), reproduced at TheOneRing.com
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.claim: Lewis notes the book balances snug firesides and good cheer for the hobbit in each reader against great valour and anguish.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis, 'The Gods Return to Earth' (1954)
claims.quote: many a snug fireside and many an hour of good cheer

claims.feature: historical and social reality within Quest
claims.claim: Auden says Tolkien uses the Quest's traditional properties while satisfying our sense of historical and social reality.
claims.source: W.H. Auden, 'At the End of the Quest, Victory' (NYT, 1956), at Anthropology of Accord
claims.quote: satisfying our sense of historical and social reality

claims.feature: hostile: class snobbery in speech; overworked cadences
claims.claim: Stimpson reads character language as class snobbery and Manlove hears overworked cadences and monotonous pitch, hostile readings Shippey and Rosebury rebut.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary reception of The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: overworked cadences

claims.feature: corpus: three lexical causes of archaicity
claims.claim: Siepmann's corpus study finds the impression of archaicity comes from overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense rare or obsolescent words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)
claims.quote: the avoidance of words associated with the modern world

claims.feature: non-standard speech marks Sam and Gollum; epic style for heroes
claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann note Sam and Gollum are marked by non-standard speech while omniscient passages shift to epic style marking Aragorn as an old-style hero.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' and 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann)
claims.quote: marked out by their non-standard speech

claims.claim: Bowman notes the Red Book device puts the tale inside quotation marks, casting Tolkien as translator rather than author.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: inside quotation marks

claims.feature: Shippey on delivered archaism and metre
claims.claim: Shippey remarks that Tolkien's lines are archaic though persuasive when delivered with conviction, and that Tolkien became very strict about metre.
claims.source: Writers Write, 'Talking LOTR With Tolkien Expert Professor Thomas Shippey'; Tolkien Library Shippey chat
claims.quote: archaic though they often are

claims.claim: Gandalf's telling of Isildur's death uses paratactic clause structure and unfamiliar proper nouns to sound sombre and chronicle-like.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Tolkienian Style
claims.quote: He leaped into the waters, but the Ring slipped

claims.claim: The Prologue's subtitle 'Concerning Hobbits' adopts a nineteenth-century antiquarian register, and the early chapters carry more place-names than The Hobbit to signal expansion.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Tolkienian Style
claims.quote: Concerning Hobbits

claims.feature: register shift Book IV to Book V
claims.claim: The prose rises from hobbit-colloquial in Book Four to a heroic register in the Pelennor chapters of Book Five.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings (Substack, 2026-08-12)
claims.quote: the hosts of Mordor wailed, and terror took them

claims.claim: A long sentence tracks difficult movement and short sentences then supply details; the Barrow-downs and Dead Marshes rely on word-sound, alliteration and understated rhyme.
claims.source: Alun Ephraim, cellar door
claims.quote: alliteration, an understated bit of rhyme

claims.claim: The Aragorn/Boromir/Elrond exchange is an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness that could not be mistaken for Capitol Hill, and Boromir's slight whine is characterising.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (1973)
claims.quote: an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness

claims.claim: Le Guin's judgement that Tolkien's plain English is direct, concrete and simple is quoted and endorsed by a language blogger.
claims.source: Stan Carey, Sentence first (2024-10-16)
claims.quote: no ichor; everything is direct, concrete and simple

claims.claim: Tolkien selects registers to suit peoples: simple and modern for hobbits, more archaic for Dwarves, Elves and Rohirrim, with hobbits mediating for the modern reader (Turner).
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style
claims.quote: simple and modern for Hobbits

claims.claim: Shippey reads Saruman's vocabulary as empty politician-speak built on words like 'real' and 'ultimate'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Shippey)
claims.quote: we can bide our time, we can keep

claims.claim: Walker's book argues the prose is strikingly invitational, taut with semantic ambiguity that widens meaning and draws the reader into sub-creation.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Walker)
claims.quote: strikingly invitational

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann find about 85% of narrative time focalized through the four hobbits, with character viewpoint conveying state of mind while omniscient narration stays vivid; the epic style is archaic diction plus parataxis linked by 'and'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings (Kullmann/Siepmann)
claims.quote: parataxis with clauses linked with 'and'

claims.claim: The corpus study finds the impression of archaicity comes from overuse of nineteenth-century-fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and obsolescent words, across four lexical sets (landscape, direction, warfare, descriptive verbs).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation (Birmingham CL2017)
claims.quote: three simple lexical causes

claims.claim: Shippey notes The Hobbit's narration see-saws between Bilbo's 'business manner', the narrator's matter-of-fact tone and Thorin's high style, with 'of course' and 'as you probably know' hinting at hidden depths.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien blog, review of Author of the Century
claims.quote: business manner

claims.claim: Théoden's 'Nay, Gandalf!' speech uses only words still current; its archaism is in the sentence arrangement, and the final clause order carries a thought modern idiom cannot (quoting Letter 171).
claims.source: Oakley Gordon, Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing (Salka Wind, 2021-12-24)
claims.quote: terser, more vivid, and sometimes nobler than modern English

claims.claim: In the Athrabeth Finrod moves deliberately between formal 'you' and intimate 'thou' to open and close distance with Andreth, encoding relationship in grammar.
claims.source: Sparrow F. Alden, Early Modern English Inflectional Morphology (Mythmoot II, 2013)
claims.quote: Finrod uses the different inflections to connote

claims.claim: Mythgard forum posters treat thee/thou in the Silmarillion as the familiar form that nonetheless sounds formal today, note Yea/Nay as the cheap archaism, and grade the Valar most archaic with First-Age Elves one step down.
claims.source: Mythgard Forums, Modern Turns of Phrase and Archaic Language (2019)
claims.quote: Yea/Nay for Yes/No

claims.claim: The omniscient narrator reappears on the Downs to raise and simultaneously discount supernatural possibility, calling the standing stone 'more like a warning'.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Fog on the Barrow-downs
claims.quote: more like a warning

claims.claim: Le Guin's essay, as summarised, reads the narrative as pulsing between polarities (darkness/daylight, confusion/clarity, imprisonment/freedom), each reversal recurring three or four times per chapter, and hears a Beethoven finale when the closing lines are read aloud.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings (LiveJournal)
claims.quote: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat.

claims.claim: 'No living man am I' opens with negation then affirmation, 'Éowyn I am, Éomund's daughter' is a pre-duel self-naming challenge, and the closing conditional is parallel and archaic.
claims.source: middle-earth-mythopoeia (Tumblr)
claims.quote: Éowyn I am, Éomund's daughter

claims.claim: 'Where now the horse and the rider?' adapts the Wanderer's ubi sunt lament, rephrasing its opening question and expanding it item by item.
